items.title: Doc Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 28, 1995
items.q: And Mario and I played with Cab together. And Mario liked the way I played. He says, “Cheat, I’m going to organize a band,” and he says, “and I want you as my trumpet player.”

ctx.x: They have some — did it take you a while for you to get used to the rhythms?

Oh, I was fired. I was fired the first time I joined Machito. Because Mario was the leader of that band. And Mario and I played with Cab together. And Mario liked the way I played. He says, “Cheat, I’m going to organize a band,” and he says, “and I want you as my trumpet player.” I said, “fine.” So I joined Mario when he left Cab the first time, and when I was in the band, he had me in the band, he had me play and he fired me the same night because I couldn’t get those rhythms to save my life. He fired me, very…

band there until I learned, and stayed there until I learned the beat. And then after I learned the beat, Mario hired me back, and I stayed in the big band a long time. But it’s hard, it’s difficult. Nothing easy about it. But I feel now I could play. But Dizzy, he came in there and he broke all that up. Now he started his type of playing in the Latin bands, and that’s what they’re doing today most of them. You hear those arrangements, they have the Latin, I mean the bebop stuff in there. And that’s what it is.…

items.title: 61124_Mario Bauza oral history interview
items.q: He stay with my band about five, six years, play well.

ctx.x: -- he played with Calloway, and then he --

He play (inaudible) in my band. He stay with my band about five, six years, play well. He's a hell of a Dixieland man. He's one of the best left. He was -- I used to admire Cheetam -- I used to hear Cheetam in the record. I told you about McKinley's Cottonpickers. He was the first trumpet player in that band. He used to play songs in that band.
